paragraphs.text: A relation of the marches and campings of the Israelites from Egypt to Canaan, Num 33:1-49. They are commanded to drive out the Canaanites, and destroy their pictures, molten images, and high places, and to divide the land by lot, Num 33:50-54. The Canaanites, if not dispossessed, should trouble and vex them; and God would do to them as he thought to do to the others, Num 33:55-56.
i.e. in great number and exact order, as armies march, and they did, Exo 12:37,38 13:18.

would have this done, partly to evince the truth of the history, partly to preserve the remembrance of God’s glorious and miraculous works both of judgment and mercy towards his people, and thereby to confirm their faith in their present difficult undertaking.
They all repaired to
by Moses’s order from all parts of the land.
See Exo 14:8 Num 15:30.
paragraphs.anchor: In the sight of all the Egyptians

paragraphs.text: either,

1. Their princes and rulers, who are sometimes called gods in Scripture; and so this is added by way of amplification, God slew their first-born; not only of the meaner sort, but even of their king and princes. Or,

2. Their false gods, to wit, those beasts which the brutish Egyptians worshipped as gods, which were killed with the rest, for the first-born both of men and beasts were then killed, Exo 13:5. See Poole "Exo 12:12"; See Poole "Exo 18:11".
a place in the wilderness of Paran, near Kadesh-barnea.
Called more fully Beeroth-bene-jaacan, Deu 10:6.
Called Gudgodah, as Jotbathah is called Jotbath, Deu 10:7.
A place upon the Red Sea, as appears from 1Ki 9:26 22:48

rather Ijim, i.e. the heaps, as the word signifies, even the heaps of Abarim, last mentioned; the Hebrew word is the same with Ije, Num 33:44, only there it is in the construed, and here in the absolute, form. Dibon-gad; so called partly by way of distinction of this from another Dibon, in the portion of Reuben, Jos 13:17, and partly, because it was rebuilt by the tribe of Gad.
Of which see Num 27:12 Deu 32:49,50 34:1
called Shittim, Num 25:1, and here Abel-shittim, for the grievous mourning which there was both for the heinous crimes committed, and horrible judgments there inflicted.
not by banishing, but by destroying them, as it is explained, Deu 7:1,2, and elsewhere. Their pictures seem to have been stones curiously engraven, and set up for worship. See Deu 16:22.
See Exo 23:24,32 Deu 7:5.
i.e. by a metonymy, the chapels, altars, groves, or other means of worship there set up, for the hills themselves could not be destroyed by them. See Poole "Deu 12:2".
i.e. both vexatious and pernicious, for the eye is a tender part, and a wound there is very mischievous.
